title: Why the Indians do it: ego, following and second line
summary: Cahn calls it a good time and an ego trip with big followings; the sound is a small part of the culture and Indians exist only in New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Get back to the structure of the Indians. We talked about the criteria for entrance. Why do you think they do it? Is it just to have a good time?

It's a good time, makes them a big man in the neighborhood, and like many, many things, it's an ego trip. These costumes have a tremendous admiration, and each of these tribes have a very large following. As you'll hear on the tapes and so forth, a lot of the music is done by the following or the second line. And they'll have a, as they march down the street, they really don't march alone.
What do you mean following the second line? Maybe we could...

The people that are following them and admiring them and cheering them on, telling them how nice they look, telling them how great they are. You'll have to really see it to appreciate it. The sound is just a minute portion of the Indian culture.
Are the Indians only found here in New Orleans?

The only place that I know of. Because you don't have much Mardi Gras in other places. I don't think they are part of the Mobile Mardi Gras, the Opelousas Mardi Gras, or wherever else they have Mardi Gras. Certainly not in the European.
